ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure is a hollow cylinder with a vertical central axis; the student is drawn with a red simple diagram at the inner wall on the right side of the cylinder, with mass m labeled beside it. The horizontal radius from the central axis to the inner wall of the cylinder is labeled r, and at the bottom there is a red curved arrow labeled with angular velocity omega, indicating that the cylinder rotates around the vertical axis. The student is stuck to the side wall, and the feet do not rely on the ground for support. Reasoning: Analyze the forces on the student in an inertial frame. In the horizontal direction, the normal force N of the cylinder wall on the student points toward the center of the cylinder and provides centripetal acceleration, therefore N = m omega^2 r. In the vertical direction, gravity mg is downward; because the student has a tendency to slide downward, the static friction force is upward. Under the critical condition of just not sliding downward, the maximum static friction force f_s = mu N, and it exactly balances gravity: mu N = mg. Substituting N = m omega^2 r gives mu m omega^2 r = mg. Canceling m, solve to get omega^2 = g/(mu r), so the minimum angular velocity is omega_min = sqrt(g/(mu r)).

raw_record.question_text: A ride at an amusement park consists of a hollow cylinder with a student placed against the wall as shown. When the cylinder rotates quickly enough, the student is able to lift her feet off the floor and remain stuck to the wall. In terms of the student's mass \( m \), the radius of the cylinder \( r \), the coefficient of static friction \( \mu \) between the student and the wall, and fundamental quantities, determine the minimum rotational velocity \( \omega \) that the ride can have while still allowing the student to stick to the wall and not slide down.

method.method_draft: Use an inertial-frame free-body diagram. First read the image: the student of mass m is pressed against the inside wall of a vertical rotating cylinder; the radius from the central axis to the wall is labeled r, and the cylinder rotates with angular speed omega about the vertical axis. From the text, note that the feet are lifted, so the floor provides no support, and static friction with coefficient mu must prevent downward sliding. In the inertial frame, the horizontal inward force on the student is the wall's normal force N, and it supplies centripetal acceleration: N = m omega^2 r. Vertically, the only upward force is static friction f_s, which at the threshold of not sliding down is maximal: f_s = mu N. Set the limiting upward friction equal to the weight mg: mu N = mg. Substitute N = m omega^2 r to get mu m omega^2 r = mg, cancel m, and solve for the minimum angular speed: omega_min = sqrt(g/(mu r)).

method.method_draft: Use the rotating frame of the cylinder and impose static equilibrium. First read the image: the student is stationary relative to the rotating cylinder wall, the wall is at radius r from the central vertical axis, and the cylinder has angular speed omega. From the text, the student has no floor contact and must not slide down, with static friction coefficient mu between student and wall. In the rotating frame, the student is at rest, so include a fictitious outward centrifugal force m omega^2 r. The wall exerts an inward normal force N that balances this outward fictitious force, so N = m omega^2 r. The student's weight mg acts downward, and static friction acts upward along the wall. For the minimum omega, friction is just at its maximum value: f_s,max = mu N = mg. Therefore mu(m omega^2 r) = mg, giving omega_min = sqrt(g/(mu r)).
